title: AI scams in Georgia and South Florida: How scammers use deepfakes to steal millions

reading.body:
This incident shows impersonation at scale, enabled by deepfake and voice cloning technology deployed without any authentication layer. Scammers created synthetic media that replicated the identity of a real immigration attorney and used it on social media to solicit money from immigrants seeking legal services. The system failure was not in the AI technology itself, but in the absence of any verification mechanism on social media platforms or in victims' processes to confirm they were speaking to the genuine service provider.

What made the fraud possible was the combination of accessible AI tools for voice and image synthesis, social media's lack of identity verification for legal service providers, and the urgency that scammers manufactured in their approach. Catching this would have required either platform-level verification of professional identity, consumer practices that treated unexpected solicitations with skepticism regardless of seeming authenticity, or both.

It is not established whether the social media platforms where these scams occurred had any specific technical or policy failures that enabled them, nor whether any particular AI systems were misused by design or merely used for purposes they were not built to prevent.

summary:
Scammers are increasingly using artificial intelligence and deepfake technology to steal millions of dollars by impersonating trusted individuals. According to the FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report, Americans reported nearly $893 million in AI-enabled scam losses last year. In Georgia, there were 71 AI-related complaints resulting in over $10.4 million in losses, while Florida reported 350 complaints with nearly $39.9 million in losses. Notable cases include a South Florida immigration attorney whose voice was cloned to target immigrants and a Cobb County couple who lost approximately $800,000 in a cryptocurrency scam.

Criminals are using AI to clone voices from social media, create fake photographs, spoof phone numbers, and research victims' family relationships to make scams more convincing. These tactics are making common fraud schemes like romance scams, emergency calls, and the grandparent scam increasingly difficult to detect. Experts recommend establishing code words with family members, verifying urgent requests through known phone numbers, and avoiding immediate responses to unexpected money requests. As AI tools become cheaper and more accessible, investigators warn the technology will continue evolving, making verification rather than speed the strongest consumer defense.
